difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: a single concept (counting grid entries against an inclusive threshold) done with one direct count in under a minute.
stem:
A $4 \times 4$ digital image has pixel intensities ($U$) as shown in the figure. The number of pixels with $U \le 4$ is:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\
\hline
4 & 7 & 3 & 3 \\
\hline
5 & 5 & 4 & 4 \\
\hline
6 & 7 & 3 & 2 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

solution.quick: Count the cells whose value is at most 4, **including** 4. Row by row this gives $4 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 11$. As a check, only 5 of the 16 pixels exceed 4, and $16 - 5 = 11$. Answer: **(C)**.

steps.title: Read the condition carefully
steps.body: $U \le 4$ means the intensity is **0, 1, 2, 3 or 4**. The value 4 itself counts, because the inequality is not strict.

steps.title: Cross-check using the complement
steps.body:
The pixels with $U > 4$ are 7 (row 2), 5 and 5 (row 3), and 6 and 7 (row 4). That is $5$ pixels, so

$$
16 - 5 = 11.
$$

Both counts agree.

solution.teaching:
**A digital image is a matrix of numbers.** A grayscale image of size $m \times n$ stores one intensity value per pixel. Here there are $4 \times 4 = 16$ pixels. Each has an integer intensity, and in this grid the values range from 0 to 7.

**Thresholding.** Many image-processing and data-analysis tasks ask "how many entries satisfy a condition?". Applying $U \le 4$ to every pixel turns the image into a **binary mask** (1 where the condition holds, 0 elsewhere), and the answer is the number of 1s in that mask:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1&1&1&1\\ \hline 1&0&1&1\\ \hline 0&0&1&1\\ \hline 0&0&1&1\\ \hline\end{array}\quad\Rightarrow\quad 11 \text{ ones}.
$$

**Histogram and cumulative count.** A histogram lists how many pixels take each intensity value. The number of pixels with $U \le t$ is the **cumulative** histogram at $t$, which is the discrete analogue of a cumulative distribution function. Dividing by 16 gives the empirical probability $P(U \le 4) = 11/16$.

**Strict vs non-strict inequalities.** $\le$ includes the boundary value and $<$ excludes it. With three pixels of intensity exactly 4, confusing the two changes the answer from 11 to 8, and 8 is one of the options.

**Counting tip.** When most entries satisfy the condition, count the entries that **fail** it and subtract from the total. It is quicker and gives an independent check.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: 3 is the number of pixels with intensity **exactly** 4 (or exactly 3), not the number with $U \le 4$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: 8 is the number of pixels with $U < 4$ ($2 + 1 + 2 + 3$). You get it if you treat $\le$ as $<$ and leave out the three pixels of intensity 4.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Row-wise the count is $4 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 11$, and the complement gives $16 - 5 = 11$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: 9 is two short of the correct count. It does not correspond to a correct count of $U \le 4$ and would come from missing qualifying pixels.

solution.shortcut: Count the complement instead. Only five pixels exceed 4 (7, 5, 5, 6, 7), so the answer is $16 - 5 = 11$.
solution.commonTrap: Reading $U \le 4$ as $U < 4$ and leaving out the three pixels whose intensity is exactly 4. This gives 8, which is option (B).

answerVerification.checkCode:
g=[[0,1,0,2],[4,7,3,3],[5,5,4,4],[6,7,3,2]]
print([sum(v<=4 for v in r) for r in g], sum(v<=4 for r in g for v in r), 16-sum(v>4 for r in g for v in r), sum(v<4 for r in g for v in r))  # [4,3,2,2] 11 11 8
answerVerification.notes: Row-wise count 4+3+2+2 = 11 and complement 16−5 = 11. This matches the official key (C). The strict-inequality count (8) equals distractor (B).
